DecSummary: The worker suffered a right elbow and shoulder injury when she fell at work in August 1991.  She returned to modified work in November 1992 but stopped working in June 1994 due to pain.  In June 1993, she was awarded a zero FEL award.  She was again awarded a zero FEL award at R1 in 1995.  The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer regarding benefits after June 1994.
The worker withdrew her appeal since her circumstances had changed.

The worker suffered a back injury in May 1991.  The Board discontinued VR services and s. 43(9) supplementary benefits in February 1995 after an eight-week assessment indicated that the worker had self-perceived limitations.  The Reinstatement Officer found that the assessment was incorrect.  The Reinstatement Officer reinstituted VR services and supplementary benefits as of September 1995.  The worker appealed denial of supplementary benefits from February 1995 to September 1995.
The worker suffered a shoulder injury in 1989.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic pain.

The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 1063/96 was denied.  A new medical report submitted by the worker did not constitute substantial new evidence since the worker did not provide a copy of the letter soliciting the report and since the report relied on facts that were contrary to findings of the hearing panel.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (issue in dispute) (relevance) (prior claim files); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (access to worker file) (documents not in possession of Board)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for a reference which was not relevant.  The issue in dispute was entitlement for chronic pain resulting from a back injury.  Chronic pain is a global condition which generally makes details of previous injuries much more relevant, even though they involved different body parts.  Documents from previous claim files while working for other employers were also relevant.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for a fall at home.  The Hearings Officer found that the fall was caused by residual weakness in the worker's leg related to a compensable accident.

The worker's right arm was pinned under a car in March 1982.  In June 1992, he was struck on the right wrist by a railway tie.  In September 1992, he was diagnosed with right carpal tunnel syndrome.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the carpal tunnel syndrome.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (deemed worker); Earnings basis (net average earnings) (Canada Pension Plan premiums); Earnings basis (net average earnings) (unemployment insurance premiums)
DecSummary: The worker was self-employed with personal coverage.  He appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding the earnings basis for calculation of benefits.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying partial commutation of his pension, valued at about $200,000, for the purpose of debt liquidation and vehicle purchase.
The worker suffered a low back injury in 1980 for which she was granted a 15% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying VR services after October 1992.

The worker suffered compensable accidents in 1986, 1989 and 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic pain and denying temporary benefits after August 1991.

A 25-year-old construction labourer fell a distance of four feet in 1984, suffering back, chest and knee injuries.  He was awarded a 5% pension for knee disability.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying VR services and supplementary benefits after 1995.

A student suffered a back injury in June 1992 while working at a summer job.  Benefits were discontinued in September 1992.  By that time, the worker would have returned to school.  Also, by that time, he had been authorized to return to work with accommodations.  The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer denying further benefits.
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 417/96 was denied.  [3 pages]

The worker suffered a back injury in 1989 for which she was awarded a 10% pension in 1992.  She received a s. 147(2) supplement until August 1993.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying supplementary benefits after August 1993.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (on call); In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work); In the course of employment (travelling) (emergency)
DecSummary: The worker responded to a call-in after work hours by the employer to repair a machine.  He was injured in a motor vehicle accident while on his way home.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for white finger disease, which the worker related to use of vibratory tools at work over a 20-year period.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for eyeglasses.  The evidence did not support a relationship between the accident and the worker's need for glasses.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Disability (disabled from working)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a left shoulder injury in December 1992.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a number of days between April 1993 and August 1993.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Evidence (surveillance); Temporary total disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in January 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary total disability benefits from August 1990 to November 1990.

DecKeywords: Cognitive impairment; Exposure (aluminum); Medical report (payment for); Procedure (witness fees) (doctor)
DecSummary: An electrician appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for neurological disability which the worker claimed was related to exposure to aluminum dust.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Consequences of injury (iatrogenic illness) (treatment)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in June 1990, for which he underwent surgery in November 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits after June 1992 and denying an increase in his 15% NEL award.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a foot condition.  On the evidence, the worker suffered a stress fracture from increased weight-bearing and walking at work between June 1990 and January 1992.

The worker was struck in the face by a metal plate in 1972.  In 1981, he was awarded a 1% pension for eye disability.  In 1991, the pension for eye disability was increased to 5% and the worker was also awarded a 5% pension for facial disfigurement.  In 1995, he was awarded a 20% pension for psychological disability.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits after November 1991.

DecKeywords: Chronic obstructive lung disease; Smoking; Notice of hearing (previous employer) (occupational disease)
DecSummary: The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying dependency benefits.  The worker died of cardiac arrest in 1990.  The widow claimed that the cardiac arrest was related to chronic obstructive lung disease resulting from dust exposure during the worker's work as a miner during the 1940s and 1950s.

The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer regarding the earnings base for calculation of benefits.  In Decision No. 199/96I, the Panel determined that the worker's earnings should not be based on the earnings basis for an apprentice.  In this decision, the Panel considered whether the full amount paid by the employer for room and board should be included in the worker's earnings base.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a 25% award for chronic pain.  The 25% award was at the top of Category 2 of the Board's Psychotraumatic and Behavioural Disorders Rating Schedule.  The worker submitted that he was entitled to an award within Category 3.

The worker returned to modified work in 1991 after an injury to her left shoulder and neck.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for right shoulder disability in 1992.

The worker suffered multiple facial fractures in a compensable motor vehicle accident.  He underwent a number of reconstructive surgeries.  He was awarded a 40% pension for chronic pain and a 5% pension for facial disfigurement, increased by the Hearings Officer to 8%.  The worker appealed the level of the pension for facial disfigurement.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a liver condition.  The worker was a firefighter from 1956 to 1986.  He claimed that he had a liver condition that was related to exposure to smoke.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (refusing suitable work); Chronic pain; Future economic loss {FEL}
DecSummary: The worker suffered left side and low back injuries when she slipped and fell in October 1990.  The Board denied a FEL award in October 1991 on the basis that the worker was capable of performing modified work but had chosen to withdraw from the work force.  She did receive a 16% NEL award.  The worker appealed decisions of the Hearings Officer denying a FEL award and denying entitlement for chronic pain.
The worker suffered a back injury in 1990.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for neck disability and chronic pain.

The worker felt pain in his groin in June 1989 when he caught a part that fell from a table.  He underwent surgery for a right inguinal hernia in January 1990, and for a left groin condition in February 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for the right hernia surgery but denying entitlement for the left groin surgery and denying temporary benefits from March to May 1990.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (residual weakness); Future economic loss {FEL} (eligibility); Future economic loss {FEL} (sustainability award); Future economic loss {FEL} (time periods); Supplements, FEL
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in April 1991 but was able to keep working until his employment was terminated in November 1991 as a result of the bankruptcy of the employer.  He started work for a new employer in February 1993 and worked until September 1993 when his employment was terminated.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer which granted a 15% NEL award but denied a FEL award.  The worker also appealed denial of entitlement for a thumb disability.

DecKeywords: Election; Right to sue (workers of both employers) (unidentified employer)
DecSummary: The plaintiff in a court action applied for a declaration that her right of action was not barred by the Act.  The action arose out of a motor vehicle accident in which the plaintiff, while driving a car in the course of her employment, was struck by a piece of metal thrown up by the rear wheels of an unidentified transport trailer.  The plaintiff had originally elected to receive workers' compensation benefits as a result of the accident but, with the permission of the Board, she filed a withdrawal of election and agreed to reimburse the Board for any benefits received.

DecKeywords: Damages, contribution or indemnity; Election (deemed); Right to sue (action for breach of contract); Schedule 2 employer
DecSummary: The plaintiff was employed by the city as a crossing guard.  She was injured when a street identification sign pole fell on her.  The pole was at the intersection of one street under the city's jurisdiction and another street under the jurisdiction of the regional municipality (the region).  It held signs for both streets.  By agreement, the city installed and maintained street signs and poles for the region.

A tune-up mechanic suffered from hand-arm vibration syndrome.  He returned to work with the accident employer in February 1994, with accommodation.  The worker was unable to work with vibratory tools.  An apprentice was assigned to the worker to help with aspects of the job that required use of vibratory tools.  The worker's employment was terminated in October 1994.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer breached its re-employment obligations and granting wage loss benefits under s. 37 from October 1994 to July 1995.
The worker appealed a decision of the Senior NEL Adjudicator regarding the level of his NEL award.
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 860/96 was denied.  [4 pages]
The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits for the worker's death from respiratory failure secondary to interstitial pulmonary fibrosis.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for right shoulder disability.

DecKeywords: Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (preexisting condition)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying SIEF relief for an accident.
The worker suffered a low back injury in November 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer reducing benefits to 50% and denying further VR services after March 1992.

The worker suffered a shoulder injury in 1984.  In 1990, it was determined that the worker should undergo joint replacement surgery.  A blood transfusion would be required during the surgery.  The worker decided to donate her own blood for use during the surgery.  The worker developed a condition known as dysautonomia as a result of donating the blood.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement for the shoulder condition and denying entitlement for dysautonomia.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a respiratory condition which the worker related to exposure to various substances at work.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a herniated disc which the worker related to a specific incident in May 1990 or to the nature of her work as a clerk stenographer.

DecKeywords: Future economic loss {FEL} (deemed earnings); Future economic loss {FEL} (sustainability award)
DecSummary: A production foreman suffered a crush injury to his finger in July 1991, for which he was awarded a 14% NEL award.  The employer provided modified work at no wage loss.  The worker was granted zero FEL awards in September 1992 (D1) and October 1994 (R1).  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the zero FEL awards.
The worker suffered bilateral shoulder disability in 1981 for which she was awarded a 20% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits in 1992.

The worker punctured the palm of her left hand with a small scissors in April 1986.  She received benefits until June 1986.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits after June 1986 for complaints of pain in her entire left arm and neck.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue further entitlement at the Board.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Intervening causes; Significant contribution (of compensable accident to disability)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable knee injury in 1986 and a compensable thigh injury in 1987.  He also suffered a non-compensable knee injury in 1991.  Shortly after the 1991 accident, it was found that the worker was suffering from osteochondritis dissecans.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the osteochondritis.

The worker suffered an ankle injury in 1982.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement in 1991 for plantar fasciitis and plantar calcaneal spur which the worker claimed were related to the compensable accident or to the nature of his work which required constant standing and walking on concrete.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (health care) (appliances or apparatus); Health care (appliances or apparatus) (orthopaedic bed); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Pensions (assessment) (back)
DecSummary: The worker sustained a low back injury at work in March 1986.  He was awarded a 60% pension in September 1990.  In June 1994, the Hearings Officer concluded that the worker was entitled to a pension reassessment.  The doctor who conducted that reassessment, in October 1994, concluded that the 60% award should be confirmed.  The worker appealed to the Tribunal from that conclusion.

DecKeywords: Aggravation (preexisting condition) (chronic obstructive lung disease); Exposure (methylene chloride); Impairment of earning capacity (total disability); Smoking; Pensions (AMA Guides) (respiratory impairment)
DecSummary: The worker's widow appealed a decision awarding him a 35% pension.  In December 1987, at the age of 58, the worker was exposed to methylene chloride while working.  His exposure was severe as his clothes were soaked in methylene chloride for an hour or two.  The worker had smoked a package of cigarettes per day since he was a teenager, but he stopped at the time of the accident.  The Board accepted the worker's condition as a compensable aggravation of underlying chronic obstructive lung disease.  However, in the Board's view, his respiratory condition was caused by cigarette smoking.  The worker never returned to work from the date of the accident until the time of his death in March 1993.

DecKeywords: Chronic pain; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Psychotraumatic disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered back injuries in 1986, 1987 and 1991.  He received temporary total disability benefits after the last accident until March 1992.  On appeal, the Hearings Officer denied entitlement for non-organic disability but extended temporary benefits for organic disability to July 1992 and left subsequent entitlement to the discretion of Client Services.  The worker appealed.

DecKeywords: Accident (occurrence); Cancer (sarcoma) (clear cell); Delay (onset of symptoms)
DecSummary: A police officer developed a clear cell sarcoma in his thumb in August 1969, requiring amputation of his thumb.  In 1971, he was diagnosed with lung cancer.  It was accepted that cancer of the thumb could metastasize to the lung.  The worker claimed that he suffered a thumb injury in a work-related motorcycle accident in April 1969.  However, in Decision No. 1058/96, the hearing panel found that the occurrence of the accident could not be established.
The worker suffered a low back injury in 1985 for which she was awarded a 10% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further temporary benefits in 1993.
The worker suffered a back strain in June 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits after February 1994.

The worker suffered a hernia at work in October 1990.  He was scheduled to undergo surgery for the hernia in January 1991 but he suffered a non-compensable heart attack in December 1990.  The Board developed a VR plan for the worker.  He received benefits until February 1992 and VR services until May 1992.  In July 1992, the Board found that the main reason for inability to return to work was the heart condition.  The Board decided that the worker was only entitled to benefits until March 1991, the date by which the worker would have been expected to recover had he undergone the surgery in January 1991.  As benefits had been paid until February 1992, an overpayment was created.  The worker appealed denial of benefits after March 1991.

DecKeywords: Procedure (reconsideration) (application and merits together); Reconsideration (new evidence)
DecSummary: The worker applied to reconsider Decision No. 747/96.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement to the worker for carpal tunnel syndrome.  There were significant discrepancies in the evidence as to the nature and quantity of the worker's job as an annexman.  It appeared that the medical opinions to date may have been influenced by the respective job descriptions which were provided to the doctors.

DecKeywords: Impairment of earning capacity (minimal impairment); Permanent disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered a shoulder injury in 1972.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a pension.

The worker suffered left shoulder, neck and low back pain in August 1990 while pulling a pump up from a depth of about 30 feet.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic pain.

The worker collided with a co-worker while walking down a hallway at work in June 1988.  She was off work for about one week.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits in 1989 for post-concussion syndrome.

The worker suffered back and neck injuries in 1991 when a stack of chairs fell on him.  He was granted a 17% NEL award for organic disability.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Officer denying entitlement for psychotraumatic disability and chronic pain.

DecKeywords: Supplements, FEL (Board-authorized program); Temporary partial disability (level of benefits)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a serious knee injury in April 1990.  He returned to modified work in October 1990 but was laid off due to lack of work in March 1991.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer granting benefits after March 1991.

The worker suffered a low back injury in 1989.  In 1993, he attended an eight-week assessment at the March of Dimes.  The worker was considered unemployable.  The Board then reduced benefits to 50%.  The worker claimed that he suffered a neck injury due to repetitive movements performed at the assessment.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Officer denying entitlement for neck disability.

The worker suffered back, neck, knee and shoulder injuries in a fall from a ladder in January 1991.  The worker appealed denial of entitlement for hip disability and denial of ongoing benefits after February 1991.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a dislocated shoulder which the worker claimed he suffered at work in November 1990.

DecKeywords: Causation (medical evidence) (standard of proof); Consequences of injury (iatrogenic illness) (treatment); Dysautonomia; Pensions (assessment) (dysautonomia)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a shoulder injury in 1984.  In December 1986, she was scheduled to undergo compensable shoulder surgery.  The worker was a nurse and was aware that the surgery would require a blood transfusion.  She had become aware of AIDS and problems with tainted blood, and decided to auto-transfuse two units of blood.  While giving the transfusion, her blood pressure dropped dramatically, and she later had difficulty climbing stairs due to dizziness.  The worker's condition was diagnosed as dysautonomia, a disease involving the autonomic nervous system, which progressed to Shy-Drager syndrome, a multi-system degenerative disease involving the central autonomic, cerebellar, basal ganglia, pyramidal or spinal motor neurons.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the dysautonomia.
The appeal by the worker's widow from a decision denying dependency benefits was withdrawn at the widow's request.  [4 pages]

The worker lost her balance on stairs at work in December 1990.  She grabbed a railing to keep from falling, which resulted in a jerking motion to her right shoulder, arm and neck.  She was awarded a 20% pension for chronic pain.  In December 1992, her VR file was closed.  In May 1993, she underwent breast reduction surgery.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Officer denying entitlement for the breast reduction surgery and confirming closure of the VR file.

DecKeywords: Rehabilitation, medical (cooperation); Rehabilitation, vocational (program not offered by Board)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in September 1989.  In August 1991, his VR file was closed after he was found to have no residual disability.  As a result of a reassessment in November 1993, the Board found that the worker was entitled to a 10% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting only 50% benefits for temporary partial disability from August 1991 to November 1993.

An assembly line worker suffered left ulnar neuritis and left medial epicondylitis in 1989 as a result of repetitive work.  The Board granted entitlement for these conditions but denied entitlement for thoracic outlet syndrome.  The worker appealed.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion)
DecSummary: The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board which found that the worker aggravated a preexisting condition in an accident, and denied ongoing benefits.

The worker suffered a low back injury in January 1993.  He returned to work on a work trial in June 1993.  His employment was terminated one month later in July 1993.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer breached its re-employment obligations.

The worker fell in December 1985.  He received treatment in the hospital but did not lose any time from work.  Eventually, it was determined that he suffered two fractured ribs.  In 1990, the worker claimed entitlement for back disability.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the back disability.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

The worker had hearing loss in 1988 of 35 decibels in one ear and 25 decibels in the other ear.  He was awarded a .4% pension.  He also developed ear infections after starting to wear hearing aids in 1990.  He was granted an additional 2% pension for otitis externa.  The worker appealed the level of the pension.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits after June 1993.
The employer appealed a decision of the Appeals Officer denying retroactive adjustment of it NEER assessment for 1991.

The worker suffered a knee injury in 1979.  He was granted a 6% pension for right knee disability and a 3% pension for peroneal nerve deficiency, for a total of 9%.  This was increased to 12% and later to 15%.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the 15% pension.
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 665/96 was denied.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Injuring process; Arising out of employment (work relatedness test); Stress, mental
DecSummary: The worker was a self-employed insurance agent with personal coverage.  He specialized in providing health and accident coverage through a particular insurance company.  In September 1992, this company discontinued its health and accident coverage, and sold its policies to another company.  Effectively, the worker was put out of business.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a stress-related disability which resulted from these events.

The employer was appealing a decision of the Appeals Officer denying further entitlement from an accident in 1990.  In a pre-hearing telephone conference, the employer advised that there was another incident of potential significance in 1986.  The Panel did not have jurisdiction regarding the 1986 incident.  The Panel gave the employer three weeks to decide whether it wanted to continue with the appeal or return to the Board to pursue the matter of the other incident.  [6 pages]
The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for an accident in November 1987, for which the worker did not claim benefits until November 1988.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Chronic pain; Hearing loss (traumatic); Temporomandibular joint dysfunction
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision which denied him initial entitlement to benefits for left-sided hearing loss, temporomandibular joint (TMJ) pain and dental abnormalities.  The worker related these conditions to a compensable accident in January 1987, in which he was struck in the head by a van that was backing up.  The worker received various periods of benefits, including a 25% chronic pain disability award following an assessment in January 1991.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss.

The worker was appealing a decision of the Appeals Officer denying entitlement for a neck injury and denying ongoing entitlement for a back injury.  At the hearing, the worker decided to proceed only on the issue of neck disability.  The Panel was of the view that the issues of back and neck problems could not be separated.  There were also some outstanding matters at the Board.

DecKeywords: Carpal tunnel syndrome; Delay (onset of symptoms); White finger disease
DecSummary: The worker was a heavy construction carpenter for 16 years until 1992.  He started experiencing wrist pain in 1990 and was granted entitlement for left carpal tunnel syndrome.  The worker appealed denial of entitlement for white finger disease and for right carpal tunnel syndrome.
A nursing assistant suffered a low back strain from lifting a patient in September 1992.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits after May 1993.
The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting the worker entitlement for an accident.  On the evidence, the Panel concluded that the accident occurred, as claimed by the worker.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (hearing loss) (policy change); Hearing loss; Medical opinion (hearing loss) (testing procedures)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a NEL award for hearing loss.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Future economic loss {FEL} (deemed earnings); Reconsideration
DecSummary: A labourer suffered a back injury in September 1991.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that work as a flagman offered by the employer in May 1993 was not suitable and that the worker was entitled to a full FEL award from July 1993 to July 1995.  In Decision No. 55/96, the hearing panel allowed the employer's appeal.  In Decision No. 55/96R, another panel decided that it was advisable to reconsider.  The Panel now reheard the appeal.
The employer's appeal was withdrawn at the request of the employer.  [3 pages]
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue further entitlement at the Board.  [4 pages]

The worker applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 1093/96.  In Decision No. 1093/96, the hearing panel granted supplementary benefits retroactive to a date after a report was submitted to the Board and after the Board had a reasonable period of time to reconsider its findings based on that report.  The hearing panel also directed the Board to reopen VR and grant supplementary benefits under s. 147(2), and therefore made no determination on the worker's request for s. 147(4) benefits.
The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Officer denying entitlement for tinnitus which the worker claimed was related to an incident at work in 1969.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

The employer was a member of the VER experience rating program.  In 1991, it was eligible for penalty assessments under s. 103(8) of the pre-1997 Act and VER assessments.  The Board assessed a penalty of $400,000 for the years 1989 to 1991.  On appeal, the Hearings Officer concluded that the penalty assessment should be cancelled.  The Hearings Officer also determined that the VER account for 1991 should be reissued.  As a result, the Board assessed the employer an additional $200,000 for its 1991 VER assessment.  The employer appealed.
The worker's estate appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the worker's death from lung cancer.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

In Decision No. 951/96, the hearing panel directed the Board to complete a NEL assessment.  At the worker's request, the Panel clarified Decision No. 951/96 by directing the Board also to address benefit and FEL issues arising from the decision.  [3 pages]
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a respiratory condition from January 1990 to January 1991.

The worker was appealing a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding denying further VR.  The Reinstatement Officer found that the worker did not make adequate effort on a work trial.  At the hearing, the worker submitted she suffered from a further condition that made the work trial inappropriate.

DecKeywords: Alternative employment (comparable employment); Suitable employment; Rehabilitation, vocational (suitability of program); Transfer of costs
DecSummary: A long haul truck driver suffered a back injury in May 1991.  In October 1992, he was granted a FEL sustainability award and a supplement.  He was also granted a 15% NEL award.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer granting ongoing VR services and associated benefits after April 1994.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Consequences of injury (residual weakness)
DecSummary: The worker sought treatment for right epicondylitis in December 1991.  She continued to work until November 1992.  She returned to light work in March 1993.  In November 1993, she complained of left elbow pain.  After surgery in January 1994, the worker returned to a modified work program in March 1994 but stopped working after one week.  The employer appealed granting of benefits after March 1994.  The worker appealed denial of benefits for left epicondylitis.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (lunch); Independent operator (hairstylist); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendant in a court action sought an order that the Plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The Plaintiff was a hairstylist who worked in a salon which was located within the premises of the defendant, a department store.  The Plaintiff tripped on a sign which was located within the defendant's premises, but outside the salon area.  He testified that at the time of the accident he had finished with all the clients he had booked for the day and was on his way across the street to get pizza, for a late lunch, which he intended to eat back at the salon.  The plaintiff stated that the only reason he was returning to the salon to eat, was in order to clean up his work area and get his hairstyling tools.  The Plaintiff had received compensation benefits for this accident and his statement of claim pleaded that he was an employee of the defendant, in the course of his employment.

The worker was injured when he slipped and fell in January 1992.  He could not return to his pre-accident employment as a truck driver.  The employer appealed a decision of the Board not to remove certain costs of the claim from the employer's cost statement.

DecKeywords: Accommodation (undue hardship); Alternative employment (comparable employment); Postal workers (letter carrier)
DecSummary: A postal worker suffered an ankle injury when she slipped in December 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying full temporary benefits from March 1992 to April 1992.
The worker suffered a back injury while carrying a heavy bag down stairs in May 1985.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement in 1989.

DecKeywords: Reconsideration (consideration of issue); Time limits (appeal); Withdrawal (of appeal)
DecSummary: The worker applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 320/96.  In Decision No. 320/96, the worker was appealing denial of a pension on an organic or chronic pain basis.  The hearing panel noted that the worker was no longer seeking a pension on an organic basis and, therefore, made no comment on that aspect of the case.  In effect, the appeal regarding organic disability was withdrawn.

The worker suffered a right knee injury at work in January 1990 while walking up stairs.  She continued to work until April 1990 when her employment was discontinued.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits from July 1991 to September 1992, and denying entitlement for right leg disability.

The worker suffered a whiplash-type injury in 1982 and a shoulder and low back injury in 1984.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary total disability benefits from January 1990 to November 1990 and denying an increase in her 10% pension for chronic pain.

DecKeywords: Investigation by Tribunal (post-hearing); Rehabilitation, vocational (academic training)

The defendant S Co was erecting the frame for a wall at a nearby house which also was being built for L Inc.  The president of S Co and the foreman for L Inc requested help from C to raise a frame for a wall.  C and his crew, along with S Co and L Inc employees, had started to raise the wall frame when it slipped, pinning C beneath it.  C's crew had helped raise a wall structure, based on a similar request from S Co and L Inc, earlier that day.  The participation of the masonry partnership's employees had taken about ten minutes on the earlier occasion.  Helping the framers was not part of the masons' normal tasks but it had been done previously when exceptionally heavy walls were raised.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work) (employer's vehicle); Right to sue
DecSummary: The issue in this s. 17 application was whether the plaintiff was in the course of his employment at the time of a motor vehicle accident.  He lived in the Greater Toronto Area but was working on a project in Cochrane 800 kilometres away.  The weekly routine was for the plaintiff and his co-workers to drive to Cochrane Sunday evening, work 40 hours over the next four days and then return to the Toronto area on Thursday night.  They travelled in a van owned by the employer.  The workers were free to use other means of transportation, but the employer would not have paid for them.  While they were staying in Cochrane, the employer paid for the workers' accommodations but not for their food.  The accident occurred while the workers were driving back to the Toronto area on a Thursday night.

The worker laid off on July 9, due to stress-related disability.  On September 18, she was laid off as part of a general lay-off.  The maintenance supervisor was also laid off. The Board NEL adjudicator noted discrepancies between the impairment level assigned by the assessor and his narrative report.  The adjudicator referred the matter to the Board's NEL psychiatric consultant.  The Board doctor wrote two detailed letters to the assessor.  The assessor agreed that the rating should be changed to moderate.  A copy of the NEL assessment (indicating a Class 4 impairment) was sent to the worker as required by s. 42(12).  However, the amended materials (changing the rating to Class 3) were not sent.  A second assessment was not requested.  The Board granted a 30% NEL award based on the amended Class 3 designation.

He advised that he either took an intercity bus or obtained a ride with friends on Tuesdays, and returned on Fridays, and he slept on a piece of foam on a friend's floor in Etobicoke Tuesday through Thursday nights. The Panel found that the worker did not sustain an accident at work on the day his employment was terminated.  The evidence of a co-worker, who was a disinterested witness, and of the foreman dovetailed.  They both stated that the employer was unsatisfied with the worker's performance and that it was particularly bad on the day of the alleged accident.  They also stated that the worker said nothing about an accident or any back pain.  The worker's testimony, that he stayed at the work site for two to four hours in excruciating pain and that he asked the foreman twice to be taken to the hospital but on being refused did not then seek medical attention until two days later, was not believable.  The more likely scenario was that the worker invented the story when he realized he was losing his job.  [8 pages]
