The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying payment of his 10% pension as a lump sum.  There was evidence from the worker's psychiatrist that it would be to the worker's advantage to have the commutation as it would enable the worker to achieve closure and get on with his life.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for plantar fasciitis of the left foot which the worker related to the nature of her work as a cashier.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (temporary partial disability) (level of benefits); Overpayment; Temporary partial disability (level of benefits)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in April 1988.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits after March 1989.  The worker also appealed the granting of only 17% benefits for temporary partial disability from October 1988 to March 1989.
The worker was appealing denial of ongoing temporary benefits after December 1991 and denial of a permanent impairment award relating to an accident in March 1991.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Procedure (absent parties)
DecSummary: The worker did not appear for the hearing of his access appeal.  The hearing had already been adjourned once to accommodate the worker.  In the circumstances, the Panel decided to proceed by way of written submissions.  The worker was given time to submit additional information but did not do so.
The employer submitted significant medical documentation on the day of the hearing.  The material was relevant but the worker would be disadvantaged if the hearing were to proceed.

The worker appealed a decision denying her benefits, from February to April 1993, on the basis that she did not suffer a foot injury at work in January 1993.  The worker claimed that she twisted her foot when it got caught between two mats in January 1993.  She worked overtime on the day she claimed that the accident happened and on a few other days during the following week.  The worker reported the accident to her supervisor the day after she claimed that it happened and she sought treatment from the company nurse two weeks later, when the nurse observed swelling over the arch area.  However, the worker did not seek treatment from her family doctor for a foot injury until February 1993, one month after she claimed that the accident happened.  She continued to work for another week before losing any time from work.

DecKeywords: Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Withdrawal (of appeal)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further VR services.  At the hearing, he did not pursue that issue but wanted the Panel to consider the issue of the recalculation of his s. 147(4) supplement pursuant to s. 147(13).  The Panel did not have jurisdiction on this issue as the recalculation had taken place after the decision of the Hearings Officer.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Adjournment (representative availability)
DecSummary: The worker requested an adjournment of his appeal regarding access to the claim file.  The Office of the Worker Adviser wrote that it normally does not provide representation in access cases but that there were a number of allegations in this case which might cause it to make an exception.  However, due to a labour dispute, the OWA had been unable to meet with the worker.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for a number of references.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (issue in dispute) (appeal)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  The employer raised legitimate issues which it may appeal.  These were issues in dispute.  It was not necessary for the employer to have made an irrevocable decision to appeal.  [4 pages]
The worker's appeal regarding temporary benefits was withdrawn as the worker wanted to pursue entitlement to s. 147 supplementary benefits at the Board.  [4 pages]

In a pre-hearing conference call, the Panel decided that the most important witnesses for the issues on appeal were the worker and the witnesses that the employer intended to call.  It was premature to determine whether it would be necessary to obtain additional evidence from Board personnel.  [4 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  There was no evidence to support the worker's allegation of misuse of medical information by the employer.  [4 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

The employer received a 57-page addendum to the Case Description one day before the hearing.  The hearing was adjourned to allow the employer time to prepare its case based on these materials.  [4 pages]

The worker suffered a number of upper limb injuries.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits after November 1987.  On the evidence, the worker's condition had not returned to its pre-accident state.  There were no other non-compensable factors referred to in the medical reports to suggest a cause other than the worker's occupation.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue further entitlement at the Board.  [3 pages]

The hearing of the worker's appeal was adjourned to obtain clarification from the Board regarding the FEL determination in this case.  In addition, the adjournment was granted to allow the employer time to prepare for new evidence that the worker, through his new representative, wanted to call.  [5 pages]

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying retroactive adjustment of its 1989 NEER assessment outside the three-year window.  The worker suffered a back injury in April 1989.  The employer had previously accommodated the worker for a non-compensable condition.  The employer requested SIEF relief.  The Board denied the request in April 1990 on the basis that there was no evidence of a preexisting condition which contributed to the disability.  An incisive examination by a Board doctor in December 1990 led to a CT scan in March 1991 which indicated a disc protrusion and moderate degenerative changes.  This information was not communicated to the employer and the Board did not appear to consider SIEF relief.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (deemed worker); Future economic loss {FEL} (pre-injury earnings); Personal coverage (estimated earnings)
DecSummary: A worker with personal coverage appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a FEL award.  The issue related to determination of the worker's pre-accident earnings.

The worker suffered a low back injury in 1974.  He underwent L5-S1 and L4-5 discotomies and removal of a sequestered disc.  In 1977, he was awarded a 20% pension.  The level of the pension was confirmed a number of times on reassessment.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying an increase in the pension.

The worker was a bricklayer's assistant and cement mixer. The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying dependency benefits for the worker's death from obstructive airways disease.

DecKeywords: Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Reconsideration (jurisdictional error)
DecSummary: The employer applied to reconsider Decisions No. 257/96 and 257/96A.

DecKeywords: Collective agreement (seniority provisions) (bumping); Temporary partial disability (wage loss benefits) (bumping); Future economic loss {FEL} (wage loss) (bumping); Earnings basis (seniority) (bumping)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a right hand injury in July 1992, for which he was granted a 2% NEL award. The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the worker's entitlement to temporary partial difference benefits and to a FEL award.

DecKeywords: Class of employer (wholesale mercantile business); Reconsideration (consideration of issue)
DecSummary: The employer applied to reconsider Decision No. 538/96. In Decision No. 538/96, the panel found that the employer should be classified in the Rate Group for other brokers after 1993.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a facial palsy, tentatively diagnosed as Bell's palsy, which the worker related to a bee sting that occurred at work.
In accordance with Decision No. 413/96R, the worker's appeal was reheard by a panel.

DecKeywords: Cancer (lung); Chronic obstructive lung disease; Exposure (asbestos); Exposure (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons); Exposure (silica); Smoking; Steelworker
DecSummary: The worker started working for a steel manufacturer in 1966. He was diagnosed with lung cancer in 1991. The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Resolution Officer denying entitlement for lung cancer and chronic obstructive lung disease.

The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 1215/96 was denied. The hearing panel conducted the hearing fairly. On occasion, parties attempt to place irrelevant or prejudicial evidence before a decision-maker. When this happens, it is part of the function of the decision-maker make rule on the admissibility of evidence and to control the conduct of the party who is attempting to use the process to prejudice unfairly the position of the opposing party. The hearing panel properly controlled the employer's attempt to introduce potentially irrelevant and prejudicial information in violation of the Tribunal's three-week rule.

DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement; Chronic pain; Psychotraumatic disability

DecSummary: The worker died from lung cancer in 1980. In 1996, the worker's widow advised that she wanted to appeal the decision of the Appeal Board denying the widow dependency benefits. In Decision No. 966/96L, the Tribunal granted the widow leave to appeal.

DecKeywords: Reconsideration; Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation)
DecSummary: Decision No. 1093/96, which granted the worker supplementary benefits under s. 147(2) of the pre-1997 Act, from January 1997 onwards, was revoked.  A subsequent Board decision, to terminate those benefits, also was revoked as it flowed from the Tribunal decision.  On rehearing the merits, the Vice-Chair found that the worker was unlikely to benefit from VR to the extent set out in s. 147(2).  The worker was entitled to supplementary benefits under s. 147(4) of the pre-1997 Act, from the time VR services were first closed in 1994 to the present and continuing.
In Decision No. 10/96R, the Vice-Chair determined that Decision No. 10/96 should be reconsidered on the issue of whether the worker suffered a compression fracture in an accident in 1990.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (job search); Supplements, FEL

DecSummary: Pursuant to Decision No. 1026/96R, the Vice-Chair reheard the worker's appeal on the issue of entitlement to reimbursement for kitchen modifications.

DecKeywords: Harassment (sex); Harassment (stalking); Reconsideration; Stress, mental (effect of pursuing remedies)
DecSummary: The worker claimed benefits for stress-related disability resulting from sexual harassment by her supervisor. In Decision No. 806/96, the hearing panel granted the worker benefits from the time she stopped working until the date that her supervisor's employment was terminated in December 1992. The majority of the hearing panel found that, after that date, any stress was attributable to her litigation in various tribunals and the courts pertaining to redress for the harassment.

DecKeywords: Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF}; Board Directives and Guidelines (transfer of costs); Experience rating (NEER); Merits and justice (interpretation); Transfer of costs (NEER) (third party actions)
DecSummary: The employer was a gas company. A worker of the employer was injured in January 1992 when he was assaulted by a customer when he went to the customer's premises to shut off the gas supply because of safety infractions. The customer was not a Schedule 1 employer. The Board had a subrogated right of action against the customer. The Board commenced an action but later discontinued the action because it was unlikely that the customer would have sufficient assets to satisfy a judgment. The Board granted the employer 75% SIEF cost relief. The employer appealed a decision of the Appeals Officer denying transfer of the remaining 25% of the costs of the claim from the employer's NEER account.

DecKeywords: Cancer (lung) (squamous cell); Smoking; Mining (nickel); Mining (uranium); Occupational Disease Panel (hard-rock mining)
DecSummary: The worker's estate appealed a decision of the Board denying entitlement for the worker's death from lung cancer.
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 1194/96 was denied. The hearing panel considered the evidence and came to a reasonable conclusion.

DecKeywords: Cancer (lung); Mining; Procedure (reconsideration) (investigation by Tribunal); Reconsideration (new evidence)
DecSummary: The worker's estate applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 107/96. The OWA, representing the estate, submitted a new medical report which took into account a report concerning risk factors related to age that might not be accounted for in BEIR IV and BEIR VI studies previously relied on in Tribunal decisions.

The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 894/96 was denied. The hearing panel considered the evidence and came to a reasonable conclusion. There was no bias apparent on the face of the decision and no denial of a fair hearing.

The worker suffered compensable back injuries in 1982, 1984 and 1988. He suffered further back injury in a non-compensable accident in 1991. The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits in 1991.
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 949/96 was denied. The hearing panel considered the evidence and came to a reasonable conclusion.

DecKeywords: Corporation (piercing corporate veil); Re-employment (exemption) (number of workers)
DecSummary: A corporation appealed decisions of the Board finding that it and another corporation should be treated as a single employer employing more than 20 workers and that the employer breached its re-employment obligations in terminating the employment of an injured worker. In Decision No. 1012/96I, the Panel found that the Board has the jurisdiction and authority to deem two corporations to be a single employer for purposes of s. 54 of the pre-1997 Act, but only in circumstances in which there are sufficient reasons to pierce the corporate veil.
The application of the worker's widow to reconsider Decision No. 1002/96 was granted. There was new medical evidence that could affect the outcome of the appeal.

DecKeywords: Reconsideration (clarification of decision); Time limits (appeal) (previous withdrawal)
DecSummary: The worker applied for clarification of Decision No. 1156/96.
In Decision No. 586/96I, the Panel found confirmed the decision of the Hearings Officer denying the worker initial entitlement for an accident.
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 167/96 was denied. The hearing panel considered the evidence and came to a reasonable conclusion.

DecKeywords: Construction (bricklayer); Investigation by Tribunal (post-hearing); Fibrosis; Silicosis; Natural justice (procedural error) (full and fair hearing); Procedure (post-hearing evidence); Reconsideration (natural justice)
DecSummary: The worker's widow applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 1170/96, in which the hearing panel denied the worker, a bricklayer, entitlement for obstructive airways disease.

The worker was a labourer and bricklayer in the construction industry. The worker's estate appealed a decision of the Appeals Resolution Officer denying entitlement for obstructive airways disease. The appeal was dismissed in Decision No. 1170/96. An application to reconsider was granted in Decision No. 1170/96R.

The worker's estate applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 107/96, in which the worker was denied entitlement for lung cancer. The estate submitted a new medical report which took into account a report concerning risk factors related to age that might not be accounted for in BEIR IV and BEIR VI studies previously relied on in Tribunal decisions. In Decision No. 107/96R, the Vice-Chair noted, however, that the medical report indicated that it would be important for a statistician to verify various data. The Vice-Chair found that, based on the material presented, the threshold test was not met. The application to reconsider was denied. The Vice-Chair noted that the estate could bring a further application for reconsideration should it obtain the additional evidence.

The worker's application for reconsideration of Decision No. 454/96 was denied. There was no adequate explanation for the delay in filing the application of 19 years since release of the original decision. Further, new medical reports submitted by the worker were not sufficiently substantial or persuasive as to put the findings of the hearing panel into question.

The worker was injured in 1989. The Board closed VR services and denied further supplementary benefits in 1994. In Decision No. 1093/96, the hearing panel granted supplementary benefits under s. 147(2) of the pre-1997 Act from January 1997. As a result of Decision No. 1093/96, the Board granted s. 147(2) benefits until October 1998, when it found that the worker had the necessary skills to obtain appropriate work, and that, accordingly, he was also not eligible for s. 147(4) benefits.

The application of the worker's estate for reconsideration of Decision No. 119/96 was denied. The Vice-Chair noted that the application for reconsideration came about 17 years after release of the original decision. Tribunal decisions have found that delay is a factor in the consideration of a reconsideration application. In this case, new evidence submitted by the estate suggested a limited, not a strong, relationship between the worker's exposure and possible neurological symptoms. The new evidence suggested only a possible, not a probable, relationship. The new evidence was not sufficient to grant the application.

The worker's application for reconsideration of Decision No. 781/96 was denied. The Vice-Chair noted the delay of almost 20 years since the date of the original hearing. While the delay was not determinative, it was a factor to be considered. In any event, the Vice-Chair found that the hearing panel considered the evidence and came to a reasonable conclusion.
